bibliography.abstract: In urban travel, traffic congestion often results in prolonged travel times, while in-vehicle crowding causes physical discomfort. Bus passengers uniquely face dual exposure to both congestion (from shared road networks) and crowding (from shared vehicle space), which compounds health risks and undermines sustainable transport goals. Despite this, few studies examine these concurrent exposures or the socio-demographic disparities in who bears this burden, particularly critical for vulnerable populations like senior groups who may face disproportionate impacts. Using Beijing bus smart card data, we measure congestion and crowding levels to identify adverse travel patterns and infer passengers' home locations. We then apply statistical and random forest models to examine how socio-demographic characteristics shape exposure to these adverse conditions across different urban areas. The study reveals the spatial-temporal dynamics of congestion and crowding, the daily rhythms of adverse travel flow across urban spaces, and the socio-demographic characteristic disparities that shape differential exposures among senior and regular cardholders. The findings indicate that congestion concentrates in urban centers and suburban hubs during peak hours, while crowding tends to persist throughout the day on suburban-urban corridors. Urban residents experience more congestion but less crowding than suburban and rural residents. Senior cardholders experience shorter durations but higher rates of adverse conditions than regular cardholders. By revealing dual exposure patterns across space, time, and demographics, this study identifies where and when interventions are needed to reduce congestion for urban commuters and crowding for suburban riders.
bibliography.title: Examining dual exposure to traffic congestion and in-vehicle crowding among senior and regular cardholders using smart card data

en.caveats: The findings rely on smart card data to infer both passenger home locations and exposure levels, which may not capture the subjective physical discomfort or health impacts experienced by individual riders.
en.what: Using bus smart card data from Beijing, this study measures concurrent exposure to traffic congestion and in-vehicle crowding, inferring passenger home locations to analyze demographic disparities. The researchers applied statistical and random forest models to compare exposure patterns between senior and regular cardholders across urban, suburban, and rural zones. The analysis reveals that while congestion peaks in urban centers and suburban hubs during rush hours, crowding persists all day along suburban-urban corridors, leaving suburban and rural residents with higher crowding exposure.
en.why: It demonstrates that senior cardholders face shorter travel durations but experience higher rates of adverse travel conditions than regular cardholders, providing empirical evidence of age-based transit disparities to help planners target localized interventions like congestion relief in urban centers and crowding reduction on suburban routes.
